blocks.content: Recognize safe handling, storage, and disposal awareness; follow local procedures.

items.definition: Hazardous materials must be disposed of by following EPA and local regulations, using licensed disposal vendors, and NEVER pouring chemicals down drains or into regular trash.
items.analogy: Like recycling electronics — you can't toss a laptop in the garbage; it must go through a certified e-waste vendor.

items.definition: Nickel-Cadmium (NiCd) batteries must be disposed of by following local hazardous materials regulations — they CANNOT be discarded in regular trash because cadmium is a toxic heavy metal.
items.analogy: Like old paint — you can't toss it in the garbage. It must go through an approved hazmat collection event or licensed disposal service.

items.definition: The document required to be readily available for each hazardous material used in a Part 145 avionics shop — covering hazards, PPE requirements, first aid, and disposal procedures.
items.analogy: Like a medication package insert required by law — it must be on hand and tells you exactly what you are working with and what to do if something goes wrong.

items.definition: For a hydraulic fluid spill near avionics equipment: (1) contain immediately with absorbent materials, (2) remove power from nearby equipment, (3) clean up following shop hazmat procedures.
items.analogy: Like a kitchen grease fire — contain it first, cut the ignition source (power), then clean up properly.

blocks.question: Which method is acceptable for disposing of used solvent in a GA avionics shop?
choices: Pour it down the utility sink drain
Absorb it and place in regular trash
Use a licensed hazardous waste disposal vendor per EPA and local regulations
Evaporate it outside away from the building
blocks.feedback: Hazardous chemicals must go through licensed disposal vendors following EPA and local regulations — drains and regular trash are prohibited.

blocks.question: An aircraft NiCd battery has reached end-of-life. What is the correct disposal procedure?
choices: Discharge fully and place in regular trash — it is inert when empty
Puncture the cells for safe venting before disposal
Follow local hazardous materials disposal regulations — do not put in regular trash
Return it to the original manufacturer only — no other method is allowed
blocks.feedback: Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal — NiCd batteries must go through regulated hazmat disposal channels regardless of state of charge. Regular trash disposal is prohibited.

blocks.question: What document must be readily available for each hazardous material used in a Part 145 avionics shop?
choices: The FAA type certificate for the specific material
The shop's hazmat storage insurance documentation
blocks.feedback: OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard requires SDS documents to be readily accessible for all hazardous chemicals in the workplace. This applies to solvents, conformal coatings, flux, and other chemicals. No FAA type certificate exists for chemicals.

blocks.question: Hydraulic fluid spills onto the avionics bench area. What is the correct immediate response?
choices: Wipe it up quickly with shop rags and continue work
Contain the spill with absorbent materials, remove power from nearby equipment, then clean up per hazmat procedures
Dilute the spill with water to reduce fire risk before cleaning
Only clean up after the current job is completed to avoid work interruption
blocks.feedback: Hydraulic fluid is flammable and corrosive. You must contain it first, remove electrical power (ignition hazard), then follow established hazmat cleanup procedures.
